NSAID (ibuprofen / naproxen) for short-term flares with PPI cover. Low-dose prednisolone 5–10 mg daily as bridging in early disease; intra-articular methylprednisolone for mono-articular flares. AVOID long-term steroid where possible.

Stop methotrexate ≥ 3 months pre-conception (both partners). Sulfasalazine / hydroxychloroquine / TNF inhibitors generally safe in pregnancy. Disease flares are common postpartum — reinstate DMARD early.
Annual CV risk assessment (RA confers excess risk equivalent to diabetes); statin if QRISK > 10 %. Bone-density scan if chronic steroid > 3 months / postmenopausal.

references.label: EULAR Recommendations for management of RA (2022 update)
NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis in adults (2018)

title: Obesity (adult)
presentation: Body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m² (≥ 27.5 in South / East Asian descent — WHO 2004 modifier).
Increased waist circumference (≥ 102 cm men / ≥ 88 cm women) = central obesity.
Often co-exists with T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, MASLD, OSA, osteoarthritis, depression.
redFlags: Class III obesity (BMI ≥ 40) — high anaesthetic / perioperative risk.
Symptoms of secondary cause: hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, hypothalamic disease, medication-induced (steroid, antipsychotic).
Severe obstructive sleep apnoea — daytime sleepiness, witnessed apnoeas, BP control resistant.

diagnostics.rationale: BMI for class; WC adds CV risk discrimination.

diagnostics.test: Fasting glucose / HbA1c + lipids + LFT + TSH + cortisol where indicated
diagnostics.rationale: Diagnose comorbidity + exclude secondary causes.
Screen for OSA.

management.detail: Energy-deficit diet (500–750 kcal/day below baseline). Mediterranean or low-carb pattern acceptable. ≥ 150 min/week moderate aerobic + resistance training 2 days/week. Behavioural therapy + group support increase success. Target 5–10 % weight loss in 6 months.

After 6 months of lifestyle. Options: orlistat 120 mg three times daily with meals (GI side effects); GLP-1 receptor agonists — liraglutide 3 mg SC daily or semaglutide 2.4 mg SC weekly (mean weight loss 10–17 %). Bupropion-naltrexone, phentermine-topiramate alternatives.

BMI ≥ 40 OR ≥ 35 with comorbidity (T2DM, OSA, HTN). Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy — average 25–30 % total weight loss + diabetes remission rates 40–80 %. Lifelong vitamin / mineral supplementation.
Treat T2DM (metformin + GLP-1 RA / SGLT2i preferentially for weight benefit). Statins per CV risk. CPAP for moderate-severe OSA. Mental-health support — depression highly co-morbid.

Pre-conception weight loss reduces gestational diabetes / pre-eclampsia / large-for-gestational-age. AVOID weight loss in pregnancy itself. Folic acid 5 mg pre-conception in BMI ≥ 30 (higher NTD risk).

references.label: NICE CG189 — Obesity: identification, assessment and management (2014)

title: Chronic functional constipation (adult)
presentation: Rome IV criteria: 2 or more of — straining > 25 % of defaecations, lumpy / hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual manoeuvres, < 3 spontaneous bowel movements per week — for at least 3 months with onset > 6 months ago.
Loose stools rare without laxatives.
Insufficient criteria for IBS.
redFlags: Age ≥ 50 with new constipation — exclude colorectal cancer (colonoscopy).
Rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss.
Family history of colorectal cancer / IBD.
Severe abdominal pain — exclude obstruction / ischaemic colitis.
Faecal impaction with overflow — disimpaction priority.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical without alarm features.
Rule out anaemia, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes.
All alarm features; over 50 with new constipation.

management.detail: Dietary fibre 25–30 g/day (gradual increase to avoid bloating). Adequate fluid intake. Regular physical activity. Toileting routine — 15–30 min after meals (gastrocolic reflex), unhurried, knees above hips (Squatty Potty).
Ispaghula husk (psyllium) 3.5 g sachet 1–3 times daily with fluid. Avoid in opioid-induced constipation / faecal impaction / mechanical obstruction.
Polyethylene glycol (Movicol) 1 sachet 1–3 times daily — first-line per NICE. Lactulose 15 mL twice daily — useful in hepatic encephalopathy too.
Senna 7.5–15 mg at night OR bisacodyl 5–10 mg at night — short-term use only, evidence supports safety for chronic use in opioid-induced constipation.
Disimpaction first: oral PEG high-dose (8 sachets in 1 L water over 6 h, repeat × 3 days), OR sodium-phosphate enema, OR manual disimpaction. Maintenance laxative once cleared.
Stimulant + osmotic combination from start of opioid. PAMORA (naloxegol, methylnaltrexone) for refractory cases.
After failure of 2 laxative classes at adequate dose. Consider colonic transit study, anorectal manometry, biofeedback for dyssynergia.

references.label: ACG Guideline on Chronic Idiopathic Constipation (2021)

title: Acute pancreatitis (adult)
presentation: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to back, often relieved by leaning forward.
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal tenderness, distension, reduced bowel sounds.

Causes (I-GET-SMASHED): Idiopathic, Gallstones (50 %), Ethanol (25 %), Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion, Hypercalcaemia / Hypertriglyceridaemia, ERCP, Drugs (azathioprine, valproate, GLP-1 RA).
redFlags: Glasgow / Atlanta severity criteria — > 3 of: age > 55, WCC > 15, glucose > 10 (non-diabetic), urea > 16, PaO₂ < 8 kPa, calcium < 2.0, albumin < 32, LDH > 600 = severe.
SIRS, persistent organ failure > 48 h = severe acute pancreatitis (mortality 15–25 %).
Grey-Turner / Cullen sign (haemorrhagic), shock, AKI, ARDS.
Necrotising / infected pancreatitis on CT at 72 h.

diagnostics.test: Serum lipase or amylase × 3 upper limit of normal
diagnostics.rationale: Lipase more sensitive + specific; amylase falls within 3–5 days.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, magnesium, LDH, CRP, LFT, lipid profile, ABG
diagnostics.rationale: Severity assessment + cause identification (Glasgow score).
Gallstones, biliary dilation, CBD stones.
Severity assessment + complications (necrosis, fluid collections). Not for diagnosis.

management.detail: Lactated Ringer's 5–10 mL/kg/h for first 24 h, titrated to urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h. Most important early intervention.
Strong opioid — morphine 5–10 mg IV every 4 h or PCA. (Historic concerns about morphine + sphincter-of-Oddi spasm not borne out clinically.)
Metoclopramide 10 mg IV every 8 h or ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 h. NG tube if persistent vomiting / ileus.
Early enteral feeding (within 24–72 h) — oral if tolerated, NG / NJ if not. NPO not evidence-based beyond first 24 h. Reduces infection + mortality.
NOT routinely indicated even in severe pancreatitis. Reserve for confirmed infected necrosis (FNA-proven) — meropenem 1 g IV every 8 h.

Gallstone pancreatitis: ERCP + sphincterotomy within 72 h if cholangitis / persistent obstruction; cholecystectomy same admission. Alcohol: support to stop drinking. Hypertriglyceridaemia: fibrate + insulin / heparin if severe.
Organ failure > 48 h, severe by Glasgow score, infected necrosis, persistent shock.

title: Herpes zoster (shingles, adult)
presentation: Prodromal pain, burning or paraesthesia in a dermatomal distribution (1–5 days before rash).
Vesicular rash in a single dermatome, often thoracic; does not cross midline.
Painful, weeping, then crusts in 7–10 days.
Risk factors: age > 50, immunosuppression, stress.
redFlags: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1 — nasociliary branch / Hutchinson's sign — vesicles on nose tip) → urgent ophthalmology, risk of corneal scarring + blindness.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (vesicles in ear / facial palsy / vertigo) — same-day ENT / neurology.
Disseminated zoster (> 20 vesicles outside primary dermatome) — immunocompromised; admit IV aciclovir.
Post-herpetic neuralgia — persistent pain > 90 days; 10–15 % of cases.

diagnostics.rationale: Dermatomal vesicular rash is characteristic.
Atypical presentation, immunocompromised, eye / ear involvement.
Atypical / recurrent / disseminated zoster in < 50 — high-yield.

management.step: Oral antiviral within 72 hours of rash onset
management.detail: Aciclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 7 days, OR valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days (better bioavailability). Reduces severity, duration + PHN risk.
Paracetamol + NSAID; add amitriptyline 10–25 mg at night OR gabapentin titrated for severe acute pain. Avoid topical steroids.
Keep lesions clean, dry, covered. Counsel against contact with non-immune pregnant women / immunocompromised / neonates (varicella risk).
Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7–10 days + topical aciclovir 3 % eye ointment + urgent ophthalmology — risk of keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma.
Amitriptyline 10–75 mg at night, gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated to 1.8 g/day, pregabalin 75 mg twice daily. Topical lidocaine 5 % patch or capsaicin 8 % patch (specialist).
Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) — 2 doses 2–6 months apart in adults ≥ 50; also recommended for immunocompromised ≥ 19.

title: Atopic eczema (child)
presentation: Itchy chronic / recurrent inflammatory skin condition.
Infant pattern: face, scalp, extensor surfaces.
Older child pattern: flexures (antecubital, popliteal), neck, wrists, ankles.
Personal / family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy).
redFlags: Eczema herpeticum — multiple monomorphic vesicles / punched-out erosions + fever → urgent IV aciclovir + ophthalmology if periocular.
Bacterial superinfection — golden crusts, pustules, weeping, fever.
Failure to thrive / GI symptoms — investigate food allergy (cow's milk, egg).

diagnostics.rationale: UK working-party criteria — itch + 3 of: flexural involvement, history of asthma / hay fever (or in first-degree relative if < 4 y), dry skin in past year, onset < 2 y.
If superinfection / eczema herpeticum suspected.

management.detail: Generous emollient (250–500 g/week) applied at least twice daily even when skin clear. Avoid soap; use emollient as soap substitute. Tap-water bathing 10 min daily with emollient lock-in. Counsel: more is better.

Mild (hydrocortisone 1 %) face / flexures. Moderate (clobetasone 0.05 %) trunk / limbs. Potent (betamethasone 0.1 %) chronic lichenified areas — short courses only. Apply 30 min before / after emollient. One fingertip unit = palm-of-hand area.
Localised: topical fusidic acid 2 % for 5 days. Widespread: oral flucloxacillin 5 days. Eczema herpeticum: aciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 8 h + admission.
Tacrolimus 0.03 / 0.1 % ointment or pimecrolimus 1 % cream — second-line for face / flexures to spare steroids; specialist initiation.

Avoid triggers (soap, fragranced products, wool, overheating, dust mite where major trigger). Cotton clothing. Keep nails short to reduce scratching damage. Sedating antihistamine at night for severe itch in younger children.
Uncontrolled despite optimal topical therapy at 4–6 weeks; recurrent infections; eczema herpeticum; suspected food-allergy contribution.

references.label: NICE CG57 — Atopic eczema in under-12s

title: Plaque psoriasis (adult)
presentation: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, lower back.
Itch in 70 %.
Nail involvement (pitting, onycholysis) in 50 %.
Psoriatic arthritis in 10–30 %.
Comorbidities: metabolic syndrome, CV disease, depression, IBD.
redFlags: Erythrodermic / generalised pustular psoriasis — admit for fluid + temperature management + systemic therapy.
Rapid worsening on drug exposure (lithium, β-blocker, antimalarial, terbinafine, NSAID, withdrawal of systemic steroid).
Joint pain / morning stiffness → screen for psoriatic arthritis (PEST screening tool).

diagnostics.rationale: Severity scoring guides treatment ladder; PASI ≥ 10 / BSA ≥ 10 / DLQI ≥ 10 = severe.
Atypical presentations; rules out other dermatoses.
Lipid profile, fasting glucose, BP, BMI — manage CV risk.

management.detail: Daily emollient. Potent topical steroid (betamethasone 0.1 %) once daily + vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol 50 µg/g) once daily for 4 weeks (combination products available). Coal tar for scalp.
Narrowband UVB 2–3× weekly for 8–12 weeks. Avoid in skin types I, photosensitive disorders.
Methotrexate 7.5 mg once weekly titrated to 25 mg, or ciclosporin (specialist), or acitretin (avoid in women of childbearing potential).
Adalimumab, infliximab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab, risankizumab — specialist initiation, IGRA-negative, HBV / HCV / HIV screen.
Statin per CV risk, lifestyle (weight loss, smoking cessation, moderate alcohol). Screen + treat depression, psoriatic arthritis.

title: Uncomplicated gonorrhoea (adult)
presentation: Urethritis (men): dysuria, mucopurulent discharge 2–5 days post-exposure.
Cervicitis (women): often asymptomatic; intermenstrual / post-coital bleeding, mucopurulent discharge, dyspareunia.
Pharyngeal (often asymptomatic), rectal (proctitis), conjunctivitis (neonatal ophthalmia).
redFlags: Disseminated gonococcal infection — fever, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, polyarthralgia → admit, IV ceftriaxone.
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): lower abdominal pain, fever, cervical motion tenderness.
Co-infection: HIV / syphilis / hepatitis B / C / chlamydia must always be tested.

diagnostics.test: NAAT (urine / endocervical / vaginal / pharyngeal / rectal swab)
diagnostics.rationale: Highest sensitivity; multiplex with chlamydia.
Antimicrobial resistance surveillance — ESC-resistant gonorrhoea emerging globally.
Mandatory co-screening.

management.detail: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (per WHO 2021; previously 500 mg). Add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days if chlamydia not yet excluded.
Gentamicin 240 mg IM single dose + azithromycin 2 g orally single dose (sub-optimal alternative). Discuss with sexual-health specialist.
Same ceftriaxone dose; harder to cure — test-of-cure NAAT at 14 days.
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days.
Trace contacts from previous 60 days. Abstain from sex (including oral) for 7 days after treatment AND until partners treated. Provider-administered partner therapy where legal.
NAAT at 14 days for pharyngeal / rectal infection; reinfection screen at 3 months for all.

title: Uncomplicated genital chlamydia (adult)
presentation: Often asymptomatic (70 % women, 50 % men).
Men: urethritis with mucoid discharge, dysuria.
Women: post-coital / intermenstrual bleeding, abnormal discharge, dyspareunia, often subtle.
Rectal / pharyngeal often asymptomatic; reactive arthritis (Reiter triad) rare.
redFlags: Pelvic inflammatory disease — risk of infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) — invasive serovars, severe proctitis in MSM; doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days.
Neonatal conjunctivitis / pneumonia from untreated maternal infection.

diagnostics.rationale: Self-collected vaginal swab equivalent to clinician-taken.

diagnostics.test: Co-test HIV / syphilis / HBsAg / anti-HCV / gonorrhoea
diagnostics.rationale: Always co-screen.

management.detail: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. (Replaced single-dose azithromycin in 2024 due to rising azithromycin resistance.)
Azithromycin 1 g single dose OR amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days.
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days. Refer specialist.
Contact tracing from previous 6 months (last sexual partner if symptomatic). Abstain 7 days post-treatment + until partners treated.
TOC NAAT at 4 weeks for pregnancy / LGV / pharyngeal. Routine re-screen at 3 months.

title: TB preventive therapy (TPT) for latent TB infection
presentation: Latent TB infection — positive IGRA / TST without clinical or radiological evidence of active disease.

Risk groups warranting TPT (WHO 2024): people living with HIV, household contacts of pulmonary TB (especially < 5 y), clinical / radiographic risk, dialysis, prior TB on imaging untreated, silicosis, anti-TNF therapy.
redFlags: Active TB symptoms (cough > 14 days, fever, night sweats, weight loss) → rule out active TB before TPT (TPT alone in active TB causes resistance).

diagnostics.rationale: Must exclude active TB before TPT.
Confirms LTBI in low-prevalence; presumed in high-prevalence household contacts < 5 + PLHIV.
HIV co-infection changes drug interaction strategy.
Hepatotoxicity monitoring.

management.detail: Per WHO 2024: 1HP (isoniazid 300 mg + rifapentine 900 mg ONCE WEEKLY for 1 month) for adults / adolescents ≥ 13 y; OR 3HP (isoniazid + rifapentine once weekly for 12 weeks); OR 3HR (isoniazid + rifampicin daily for 3 months); OR 6H / 9H (isoniazid daily for 6 / 9 months); OR 4R (rifampicin daily for 4 months) for INH intolerance.
25–50 mg daily with isoniazid-containing regimens to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
Strongly recommended. 3HP or 6H once weekly preferred for adherence. Note rifapentine / rifampicin halves dolutegravir — double DTG to 50 mg twice daily during therapy + 2 weeks after.
Mandatory TPT after active TB exclusion — high progression risk. 3HP (≥ 2 y), 3HR or 6H.
Monthly review; ALT if symptoms (anorexia, jaundice). Counsel hepatotoxicity warning signs.

references.label: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB — Module 1: Prevention (2024)
WHO HIV Guidelines 2021 — TPT for PLHIV

title: HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)
presentation: Eligibility: HIV-negative person with substantial ongoing risk of HIV infection.

Risk indicators: serodiscordant partnership without partner suppression, sex worker, multiple partners without consistent condom use, men who have sex with men, transgender women, people who inject drugs, recent STI or post-exposure prophylaxis.
redFlags: Recent possible exposure (< 72 h) — PrEP is NOT appropriate; use post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) instead.
Acute retroviral syndrome (fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, mucocutaneous ulcers) — exclude acute HIV BEFORE PrEP start.
Renal impairment eGFR < 60 (oral TDF) — limits choice.

diagnostics.rationale: MUST be negative before initiation; repeat every 3 months. Combination Ag/Ab reduces window period.
TDF nephrotoxicity baseline + every 6 months.
TDF / TAF treats HBV — counsel risk of HBV flare on stopping.
Baseline + 3-monthly screen.
Counsel — PrEP is safe in pregnancy.

management.detail: Daily oral TDF/FTC 245/200 mg once daily — first-line, all populations. TAF/FTC alternative (better renal / bone safety; not for vaginal exposure). Event-driven 2-1-1 (TDF/FTC, 2 tablets 2–24 h pre-sex, 1 tablet 24 h after, 1 tablet 48 h after) — MSM with infrequent activity. Long-acting cabotegravir injection every 2 months — alternative.
Daily PrEP needs ≥ 4 tablets/week for vaginal protection; ≥ 4/week for anal. Educate dosing pattern, missed doses.
HIV Ag/Ab test, STI screen, adherence support, side-effect review. eGFR every 6 months. HBV status review.
TDF/FTC is safe — fetal benefit of HIV prevention. Continue 6 weeks post-partum + during breastfeeding while exposure persists.
Take daily PrEP for 2 more days after last potential vaginal / anal exposure (TDF/FTC), and 28 days for MSM-receptive exposure. Stop if HIV-positive — switch to HIV-treatment regimen.

references.label: WHO Consolidated HIV Guidelines (2021, with 2024 update)

title: Neonatal hypothermia
presentation: Axillary temperature < 36.5 °C (cold stress 36.0–36.4; moderate 32.0–35.9; severe < 32 °C).
Cool extremities, lethargy, poor feeding, weak cry.
Severe: bradycardia, apnoea, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, sclerema, shock.
redFlags: Severe hypothermia < 32 °C — high mortality; aggressive warming + supportive care.
Hypothermia + sepsis features (poor feeding, lethargy, raised CRP) — treat both pathways.
Neonatal asphyxia + therapeutic hypothermia — DELIBERATE 33–34 °C for 72 h within 6 h of birth — separate protocol.

diagnostics.rationale: Standard thermometers read floor of 35 °C; obtain reading below this.
Hypoglycaemia common in cold stress.
Cold stress in neonate often heralds sepsis.

management.detail: Skin-to-skin care with mother (Kangaroo Mother Care). Dry baby, hat, warm room (≥ 25 °C). Recheck temperature every 30 min.
Skin-to-skin + warm cot / radiant warmer. Cover with warm blanket. Treat hypoglycaemia (2 mL/kg of 10 % dextrose IV if < 2.6 mmol/L). Continuous monitoring.
Admit. Slow rewarming 0.5–1 °C/h (rapid rewarming → shock). Warm IV fluids, warm humidified oxygen, glucose 10 % infusion + bolus if low. Sepsis empirical antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin). ICU.

Warm delivery room (≥ 25 °C), immediate drying, skin-to-skin, breastfeeding within 1 h, no separation, transport with mother, warm clothing + hat, postpone bathing until thermoregulation stable (≥ 6 h post-delivery or 24 h preferred), regular temperature monitoring.

references.label: WHO Thermal Protection of the Newborn
WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children

title: Vitamin D deficiency (adult)
presentation: Often asymptomatic — detected on routine testing.
Diffuse musculoskeletal pain, proximal muscle weakness.
Osteomalacia (adults): bone pain, pseudofractures.
Risk groups: dark-skinned + low sun exposure, veiled clothing, elderly housebound, malabsorption, anticonvulsant / steroid use, obesity, exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation.
redFlags: Severe hypocalcaemia — paraesthesiae, tetany, Chvostek / Trousseau, prolonged QT, seizures — IV calcium gluconate.
Vitamin D < 12.5 nmol/L (severe deficiency) with elevated PTH + low calcium and / or phosphate — osteomalacia.

diagnostics.rationale: Deficient < 25 nmol/L; insufficient 25–50; sufficient 50–125; possibly toxic > 250.
Severe deficiency / osteomalacia features.

management.detail: Colecalciferol (vitamin D3) 50 000 IU once weekly for 6 weeks (total ~300 000 IU), OR 4000 IU daily for 10 weeks.
1000 IU daily (or 25 000–50 000 IU monthly) lifelong if risk persists. Higher 2000 IU in obese / malabsorption.
Universal supplementation 400 IU (10 µg) daily throughout pregnancy. Treat deficiency at standard doses; safe.
Co-prescribe calcium 1 g elemental daily during loading if serum Ca < 2.0 mmol/L.
Safe sun exposure 10–30 min mid-day to face / forearms several times weekly (skin-cancer-risk-balanced). Dietary sources: oily fish, eggs, fortified foods.

references.label: WHO Vitamin D Supplementation in Pregnancy
NICE NG34 — Vitamin D suboptimal status

title: Coeliac disease (adult)
presentation: Classic: chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, fatigue.
Non-classic: iron-deficiency anaemia (unexplained), osteoporosis, infertility, peripheral neuropathy, dermatitis herpetiformis.
Atypical: silent / asymptomatic, found on family screening.
Associated: type 1 diabetes (3–10 %), autoimmune thyroid disease, Down + Turner syndromes.
redFlags: Refractory coeliac disease (no response after 12 m strict gluten-free diet) → exclude malignancy (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma).
Coeliac crisis — severe diarrhoea, dehydration, electrolyte derangement (rare).

diagnostics.rationale: First-line serology. IgA deficiency in 2 % of coeliacs — false-negative tTG; check IgG-tTG or IgG-DGP if IgA-deficient. Patient must be on gluten-containing diet for ≥ 6 weeks before test.
Gold standard — Marsh classification. Mandatory before lifelong gluten-free diet.

diagnostics.test: FBC, ferritin, B12, folate, calcium, vitamin D, TSH
diagnostics.rationale: Malabsorption + associated conditions.

management.detail: Strict avoidance of wheat, barley, rye, sometimes oats (cross-contamination). Refer to specialist dietitian. Adherence essential — even small amounts (50 mg/day) cause mucosal damage.
Treat deficiencies — iron, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium. Annual review.
Symptoms + IgA-tTG at 3, 6, 12 months — should fall to normal. Repeat biopsy at 12 months if symptoms persist.
DEXA at diagnosis + repeat 5-yearly. Calcium + vitamin D supplementation if dietary intake inadequate.
Functional hyposplenism — single dose PPV23 at diagnosis.
First-degree relatives — IgA-tTG at presentation + every 5 years (10 % concordance).

title: Irritable bowel syndrome (adult)
presentation: Rome IV criteria: recurrent abdominal pain ≥ 1 day/week in last 3 months, associated with ≥ 2 of: defaecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form. Symptoms ≥ 6 months.
Subtypes: IBS-D (diarrhoea predominant), IBS-C (constipation), IBS-M (mixed), IBS-U (unclassified).
Often coexists with anxiety / depression.
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms.
Family history of colorectal cancer / IBD.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical in absence of red flags.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP / ESR, coeliac serology (IgA-tTG), faecal calprotectin
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude IBD, coeliac, malignancy, infection. Faecal calprotectin > 50 µg/g suggests IBD.
Red flags or > 50 years.

management.detail: Explain chronic relapsing course; symptoms real but no underlying organic disease in confirmed IBS. Stress management, regular sleep, exercise.
Reduce caffeine, alcohol, fatty / spicy food, fizzy drinks. Regular meals, adequate fluid intake. Low FODMAP diet (specialist dietitian) — 70 % response rate. Probiotics 4-week trial.
Soluble fibre (ispaghula husk 3.5 g 1–3× daily). Avoid insoluble fibre (bran — worsens symptoms). Macrogol (Movicol) 1–3 sachets daily. Linaclotide if refractory.
Loperamide 2–4 mg as needed (max 16 mg/day). Cholestyramine for bile-acid diarrhoea. Rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 14 days (specialist).
Antispasmodics — mebeverine 135 mg three times daily, or hyoscine butylbromide 10–20 mg three or four times daily. Peppermint oil capsules 200 mg three times daily.
CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy — Cochrane evidence. Low-dose TCA (amitriptyline 10 mg at night) — second-line for pain in IBS-D.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease — IBD (adult)
presentation: Ulcerative colitis (UC): bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue.
Crohn's disease (CD): abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, perianal disease, fistula, growth failure in children.
Extra-intestinal: arthritis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Bimodal age distribution: 15–35 and 50–70.
redFlags: Acute severe UC (Truelove + Witts): > 6 bloody stools/day + ≥ 1 of fever, tachycardia, anaemia, raised ESR → admit, IV hydrocortisone.
Toxic megacolon (colon > 6 cm + sepsis) → emergency colectomy.
Colorectal-cancer risk — annual colonoscopic surveillance from 8–10 years' duration.

diagnostics.rationale: Distinguishes IBD from IBS (> 250 µg/g supports IBD).
Diagnosis + extent; mucosal histology distinguishes UC vs CD.
Crohn's small-bowel + perianal disease.

diagnostics.test: FBC, CRP, ESR, ferritin, B12, vitamin D, U&E, LFT
diagnostics.rationale: Disease activity + nutritional status.

management.detail: Topical 5-ASA (mesalazine enema / suppository) for distal disease. Oral 5-ASA 2.4–4.8 g/day for extensive disease. Oral prednisolone 40 mg/day taper over 8 weeks if 5-ASA fails.
Oral 5-ASA 1.2–2.4 g/day. Add azathioprine 2 mg/kg if steroid-dependent or refractory. Biologic (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, JAK) for severe / refractory.

Mild ileal: budesonide 9 mg/day for 8 weeks (lower steroid side effects). Moderate–severe: prednisolone 40 mg taper, OR exclusive enteral nutrition (children — first-line). Anti-TNF + immunomodulator for high-risk.
Azathioprine 2 mg/kg + anti-TNF (infliximab / adalimumab). Specialist.
Admit. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 h × 3 days. If no response at day 3, rescue with infliximab 5 mg/kg OR ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day IV. If no response at day 7, colectomy.
Active disease worse than disease control on most therapies. Continue azathioprine + anti-TNF (specialist input). AVOID methotrexate (3 months pre-conception).
Colonoscopy annually from year 8–10. Iron / B12 / folate / vitamin D supplements. Smoking cessation (helps UC; essential in CD).

title: Bipolar disorder (adult, chronic management)
presentation: Bipolar I: ≥ 1 manic episode (lasting ≥ 7 days OR requiring hospitalisation).
Bipolar II: hypomanic episodes (≥ 4 days, less severe) + depressive episodes.
Mania: elevated / irritable mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, flight of ideas, increased goal-directed activity, risky behaviour, psychotic features in severe.
Depression in BD: longer-lasting + more episodes than mania.
redFlags: Suicidal ideation (item 9 PHQ-9) — same-day mental-health pathway. Lifetime suicide rate 15 %.
Manic episode with psychotic features / aggression — consider admission.
Mixed features (depression + agitation) — high suicide risk.
Pregnancy + valproate — major teratogen, NEVER use in women of childbearing potential.

diagnostics.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical.

diagnostics.test: TSH, FBC, electrolytes, glucose, lipids, baseline pregnancy test
diagnostics.rationale: Pre-mood-stabiliser baseline + exclude reversible causes.
Screening tool.

management.detail: Stop antidepressants. Lithium OR olanzapine OR risperidone OR quetiapine first-line. Add short-term benzodiazepine for sleep / agitation. Continue 6 months after remission.
Quetiapine OR lithium OR lamotrigine. Olanzapine + fluoxetine combination. Avoid SSRI monotherapy (manic switch + cycle acceleration). Add lithium / lamotrigine to existing mood stabiliser.

Lithium first-line (best anti-suicide evidence; serum 0.6–0.8 mmol/L). Alternatives: lamotrigine (depression-predominant), quetiapine, olanzapine, valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential).

Lithium acceptable with specialist input + level monitoring (cardiac scan at 18–20 weeks). Lamotrigine often preferred. STOP valproate pre-conception. Postpartum is highest-risk period — restart prophylaxis immediately after delivery.
Psychoeducation, sleep hygiene (sleep deprivation triggers mania), regular routine, avoid alcohol / stimulants, family-focused therapy, CBT for residual depression.
Lithium: 3-monthly level + 6-monthly TSH / U&E / Ca. Antipsychotic: BMI / glucose / lipids 3 m / annually. Screen CV risk + substance use.

title: Vitamin B12 deficiency (adult)
presentation: Macrocytic anaemia (MCV > 100 fL) — fatigue, pallor, glossitis.
Neurological — peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of cord (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts), cognitive change, depression.
Causes: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune), strict vegan diet, malabsorption (gastric surgery, Crohn's, coeliac, metformin, PPI, H. pylori), bacterial overgrowth, tropical sprue, fish-tapeworm.
Children of B12-deficient mothers — irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment if untreated.
redFlags: Severe anaemia (Hb < 7) with neurological symptoms — admit + parenteral B12.
Subacute combined degeneration — urgent treatment; recovery incomplete after weeks.
Pregnancy + deficiency — supplement urgently to prevent foetal neural-tube + neurodevelopmental impact.

diagnostics.rationale: < 148 pmol/L definitive; 148–258 borderline.
Pernicious anaemia.
Borderline B12 — both raised in true deficiency.
Macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils.

diagnostics.test: Folate, ferritin, TSH, anti-tTG, H. pylori
diagnostics.rationale: Co-deficiencies + cause.

management.detail: Hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM every 2–3 days for 2 weeks (or until improvement), then 1 mg every 3 months lifelong. If neurological involvement: 1 mg every 2 days until no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months.
Cyanocobalamin 50–150 µg orally daily. Counsel B12 sources (eggs, dairy, fortified foods). Vegans: lifelong B12 supplementation.
Folate concurrently (NEVER folate alone in B12 deficiency — accelerates neurological harm). Treat coeliac, H. pylori, dysbiosis as appropriate.
1 mg IM monthly throughout pregnancy + breastfeeding if confirmed deficient. Test infant + maintain maternal supplementation.
FBC + reticulocytes at 1 week (reticulocytosis confirms response), B12 + Hb at 8 weeks; expect full haematological recovery; neurological recovery slower over months.

references.label: BSH B12 + Folate Deficiency Guidelines (2014, updated 2024)

title: Panic disorder (adult)
presentation: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks — sudden intense fear with autonomic / cognitive symptoms peaking within 10 min: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnoea, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, derealisation, fear of dying / losing control.
Persistent worry about future attacks; avoidance of situations where attacks may occur (agoraphobia).
Often presents through emergency / cardiology services with chest pain / palpitations.
redFlags: Exclude organic mimics: thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma, arrhythmia (SVT), pulmonary embolism, asthma, cocaine / amphetamine use.
Severe agoraphobia housebound — early intervention prevents chronicity.

diagnostics.rationale: Clinical diagnosis.

diagnostics.test: TSH, FBC, glucose, urine drug screen + ECG
diagnostics.rationale: Exclude organic / drug-related cause.
Comorbid depression / GAD.

management.detail: Explain physiology of panic (sympathetic surge, hyperventilation), reassure not dangerous. Reduce caffeine / alcohol / stimulants. Regular exercise, sleep hygiene.
Cognitive behavioural therapy with interoceptive exposure — most effective evidence-based treatment. 12–16 sessions. Self-help CBT apps and bibliotherapy also have evidence.

Sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50–200 mg (start lower than depression — initial anxiety worsening). Alternatives: paroxetine, escitalopram. Allow 6–12 weeks for full effect. Continue for at least 12 months after remission.
AVOID routine use beyond bridging (< 2 weeks). Dependence + cognitive impairment + impedes CBT efficacy.
Reassurance, slow breathing (in 4 / out 6), grounding. Most attacks resolve within 30 min.
If not improving at 12 weeks of CBT / SSRI. Consider second SSRI, TCA (clomipramine), or specialist input.

references.label: NICE CG113 — Generalised anxiety disorder + panic disorder

title: Atrial fibrillation (adult)
presentation: Irregularly irregular pulse. Often asymptomatic; otherwise palpitations, fatigue, dyspnoea, syncope.
Paroxysmal (< 7 d, self-terminating), persistent (> 7 d, restored by intervention), permanent (accepted).
Causes: hypertension, IHD, valvular disease (especially mitral stenosis — common SSA), HFrEF, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, sleep apnoea, sepsis.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability (SBP < 90, pulmonary oedema, ongoing chest pain, altered mental state) → emergency DC cardioversion.
New AF + acute decompensation in mitral stenosis (especially pregnancy) — high embolic risk + pulmonary oedema.
Pre-excitation (WPW) + AF — AVOID AV-node blockers (digoxin, verapamil, β-blockers) — use procainamide / DC cardiovert.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirms AF (irregularly irregular, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves).
Paroxysmal AF / cryptogenic stroke screen.
Structural disease (LA size, LVEF, valves) — guides rhythm vs rate strategy + anticoagulation in valvular disease.
Reversible causes + pre-DOAC baseline.
Stroke risk — score ≥ 2 men / ≥ 3 women → anticoagulation. HAS-BLED for bleeding risk.

management.detail: Rate control acceptable for asymptomatic / elderly / persistent AF. Rhythm control preferred in young, symptomatic, first AF, HFrEF (recent evidence — EAST-AFNET). Early rhythm control < 1 year of AF reduces CV events.

β-blocker (bisoprolol 2.5–10 mg or metoprolol 25–100 mg twice daily) OR non-DHP CCB (diltiazem / verapamil — avoid in HFrEF). Target HR < 110 (lenient) or < 80 (strict if symptomatic). Add digoxin if HFrEF + symptomatic.

Cardioversion (electrical if unstable / urgent; pharmacological flecainide for structural-disease-free; amiodarone if structural disease). Catheter ablation specialist (pulmonary vein isolation) if recurrent / symptomatic / HFrEF (CASTLE-AF).
CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 2 men / ≥ 3 women → DOAC first-line (apixaban / rivaroxaban / dabigatran / edoxaban). Warfarin (INR 2–3) for mechanical valves / mitral stenosis. Aspirin not recommended.
Thyrotoxicosis (propranolol + carbimazole), HFrEF (GDMT), hypertension control, weight loss, alcohol moderation, sleep apnoea CPAP.

title: Deep vein thrombosis + pulmonary embolism (adult)
presentation: DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, erythema, tenderness along venous distribution.
PE: pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia, haemoptysis, syncope, hypoxia.
Risk factors: prolonged immobility, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy / OCP / HRT, prior VTE, thrombophilia, central venous catheter, COVID-19 acute illness.
redFlags: Massive PE — hypotension SBP < 90 sustained, cardiac arrest, shock → thrombolysis / embolectomy.
Submassive PE — RV dysfunction (echo) + raised troponin / BNP → consider thrombolysis.
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — massive iliofemoral DVT with limb ischaemia → urgent thrombectomy.

diagnostics.rationale: Pre-test probability; low → D-dimer; high → imaging.
High negative predictive value when low pre-test probability; raised in age / inflammation / pregnancy / cancer (not specific).
First-line for DVT.
First-line for PE (V/Q if renal failure / contrast allergy / pregnancy).
PE — S1Q3T3 / RV strain / sinus tachycardia. Troponin / BNP for severity.

management.detail: DOAC (apixaban 10 mg twice daily × 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, OR rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily × 21 days then 20 mg once daily). Duration: 3 months provoked, ≥ 6 months unprovoked / cancer, lifelong recurrent / persistent risk.
LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily — does NOT cross placenta). Continue until 6 weeks post-partum. AVOID DOACs / warfarin in pregnancy.
LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for 1 month, then 80 % dose) OR apixaban / edoxaban — comparable in stable disease. Avoid in luminal GI / GU malignancy (bleeding).
Thrombolysis: alteplase 100 mg over 2 h. OR catheter-directed / surgical embolectomy if contraindication. Resuscitate (oxygen, fluids cautiously, noradrenaline). ICU.
Low-risk PE by PESI / sPESI may be managed at home with DOAC + early follow-up.
Only if anticoagulation contraindicated (active bleeding) AND VTE present, OR recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Remove when safe.

title: Stable angina (adult)
presentation: Predictable retrosternal chest pressure / tightness on exertion or emotional stress, relieved within 5 min by rest or sublingual GTN.
Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) class I–IV based on level of activity that provokes.
Risk factors: age, male, family history, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, low physical activity.
redFlags: New-onset rapidly worsening / rest pain — UNSTABLE angina / NSTEMI workup, urgent ECG + troponin.
Crescendo angina (more frequent / severe / triggered at lower thresholds) — admit.
Decompensated heart failure, syncope, arrhythmia, mechanical complication.

diagnostics.rationale: Often normal at rest; ST depression on exertion suggests ischaemia.

diagnostics.test: Exercise tolerance test / stress echo / CT coronary angiography
diagnostics.rationale: Functional / anatomical confirmation. CTCA first-line per NICE CG95.

diagnostics.test: Lipid profile, HbA1c, FBC, U&E, TFT
diagnostics.rationale: Risk factors + reversible causes.
High-pre-test probability or for revascularisation planning.

management.detail: Smoking cessation, BP target < 130/80, HbA1c target individualised, LDL target < 1.8 mmol/L (or > 50 % reduction), Mediterranean diet, exercise 150 min/week, weight loss.
Sublingual GTN 400–800 µg for acute episode; repeat at 5 min, max 3 doses; if pain persists → 999/ED.

β-blocker (bisoprolol 5–10 mg, atenolol 50–100 mg) OR non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil — avoid in HFrEF). Long-acting nitrate (isosorbide mononitrate 30–60 mg) third-line. Avoid β-blocker + verapamil — heart block.
Ivabradine if HR > 70 + sinus + β-blocker insufficient. Ranolazine, nicorandil specialist.
Aspirin 75 mg daily lifelong (or clopidogrel 75 mg if aspirin intolerant).
Atorvastatin 20–80 mg daily; target LDL < 1.8 (high-risk) or > 50 % reduction.
PCI or CABG for refractory symptoms / left main / triple-vessel / proximal LAD / diabetic multi-vessel disease. ISCHEMIA trial — no mortality benefit over OMT in stable disease.

references.label: NICE CG95 — Chest pain of recent onset

title: Heart failure — chronic management (adult)
presentation: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, fatigue, ankle swelling, weight gain.
Classification by LVEF: HFrEF (≤ 40 %), HFmrEF (41–49 %), HFpEF (≥ 50 %).
NYHA class I–IV severity. Causes in SSA: hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, HIV cardiomyopathy, peripartum CMP, dilated CMP, ischaemic heart disease, anaemia, thyroid disease.
redFlags: Decompensation — see acute heart-failure rule (orthopnoea, weight gain ≥ 2 kg/3 days, raised JVP, basal crackles).
Renal dysfunction on GDMT — balance renoprotection vs over-diuresis.

diagnostics.rationale: Strongly negative predictive value; cut-offs vary.

diagnostics.test: TTE — LVEF + LV size + valves + RV
diagnostics.rationale: Phenotype + severity.
Arrhythmia, ischaemia, cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, TFT, ferritin, HIV (if status unknown)
diagnostics.rationale: Reversible / contributing causes.

management.detail: (1) ACE-i / ARB / ARNI: enalapril 5 mg twice daily titrate to 20 mg twice daily; switch to sacubitril-valsartan if symptomatic on ACE-i. (2) β-blocker: bisoprolol / carvedilol / metoprolol succinate / nebivolol — start low, double every 2 weeks. (3) MRA: spironolactone 25 mg or eplerenone (avoid in eGFR < 30 / K > 5.5). (4) SGLT2i: dapagliflozin or empagliflozin 10 mg daily.
Furosemide for symptom relief; lowest effective dose. Not prognostic.
Ivabradine if sinus + HR ≥ 70 despite max β-blocker. Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate for African-American / black-ethnicity HFrEF (A-HeFT). Digoxin for symptomatic HFrEF in AF or refractory.
Diuretics for symptoms, BP control, weight loss, exercise training. SGLT2i (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) now class I per ESC 2023. Loop diuretic for congestion.
ICD: primary prevention if EF ≤ 35 % despite ≥ 3 months OMT (specialist). CRT: EF ≤ 35 % + LBBB QRS ≥ 130 ms. Cardiac transplant / LVAD: refractory specialist.

Daily weights + diuretic 'yellow zone' plan, salt < 5 g + fluid 1.5 L restriction if hyponatraemic, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, influenza + pneumococcal vaccine annually, exercise rehabilitation.

title: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD, adult)
presentation: Intermittent claudication — calf / thigh / buttock pain on walking, relieved by rest within 5 min.
Critical limb ischaemia — rest pain (worse at night, relieved by hanging leg down), ulceration, gangrene.
Atypical presentations common in diabetes (neuropathy masks symptoms).
Risk factors: smoking (strongest), diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, age > 65, family history.
redFlags: Acute limb ischaemia — '6 Ps' (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold) → vascular surgery within 6 h.
Critical limb ischaemia with ulceration / gangrene — urgent vascular referral.
Diabetic foot ulcer with PAD — high amputation risk.

diagnostics.rationale: Normal 0.9–1.3. Mild PAD 0.7–0.9; moderate 0.4–0.7; severe < 0.4. Elevated > 1.3 — incompressible (diabetes) — use toe-pressure.
Confirm extent, plan revascularisation.
PAD = systemic atherosclerosis — CV mortality > 50 % at 10 years.

management.detail: Walking 30 min, 3× per week for ≥ 3 months — increases pain-free walking distance comparable to angioplasty. Smoking cessation reduces amputation and CV events.
Aspirin 75 mg OR clopidogrel 75 mg lifelong. Atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg targeting LDL < 1.4 mmol/L (post-COMPASS, ESC 2024).
BP target < 130/80 mmHg with ACE-i / ARB preferred. Diabetes — optimise HbA1c < 7 % + SGLT2i / GLP-1 RA for CV benefit.
Cilostazol 100 mg twice daily — increases walking distance (contraindicated in HFrEF). Naftidrofuryl alternative.
Endovascular (angioplasty + stent) or surgical bypass for short-distance claudication impacting QoL OR critical limb ischaemia. Vascular surgery referral.
Mandatory in diabetes + PAD. Daily foot inspection, properly fitted shoes, podiatry, no walking barefoot.

title: Syncope — diagnostic workup (adult)
presentation: Transient loss of consciousness due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterised by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery.
Types: reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus), orthostatic (drug, dehydration, autonomic failure), cardiac (arrhythmia, structural, ischaemia).
redFlags: Cardiac syncope features — exertional, sudden no warning, supine, palpitations preceding, family history sudden death, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG.
Syncope + chest pain → ACS / aortic dissection / massive PE.
Neurological focal signs / persistent confusion → stroke / seizure / SAH.
Severe injury from fall, especially head.

diagnostics.rationale: Brugada, long QT, short QT, WPW, AV block, LVH, ischaemia, prior MI.
Orthostatic hypotension: ≥ 20 mmHg SBP or ≥ 10 mmHg DBP fall.
Anaemia, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte derangement.

diagnostics.test: Echo, Holter monitor, exercise test, tilt-table test
diagnostics.rationale: Selected based on clinical suspicion. Implantable loop recorder for recurrent unexplained.

management.detail: Reassurance + counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip). Avoid triggers, adequate hydration + salt, gradual position changes. Midodrine / fludrocortisone specialist if refractory disabling.
Stop / reduce offending drugs (α-blockers, diuretics, antihypertensives, antidepressants). Compression stockings, slow position change, increase salt + fluid, consider midodrine / fludrocortisone.
Bradyarrhythmia → permanent pacemaker (sick sinus, high-grade AV block, paroxysmal AV block). Tachyarrhythmia: rate / rhythm control + ICD if VT/VF (electrophysiology referral).
Aortic stenosis → AVR (TAVI or surgical). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → ICD if high-risk (HCM Risk-SCD score). Cardiology specialist.
Admit cardiac / high-risk syncope (SF Syncope Rule, Canadian Syncope Risk Score). Discharge with safety advice if low-risk reflex / orthostatic + normal ECG + no red flags.

references.label: NICE CG109 — Transient loss of consciousness

title: Infective endocarditis (adult)
presentation: Fever (90 %), new / changed murmur, malaise, weight loss, night sweats.
Embolic phenomena — Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots, Osler nodes (rare now), conjunctival petechiae.
Strokes / brain abscess / mycotic aneurysm.
Risk: rheumatic / congenital / degenerative valve disease, prosthetic valve, IV drug use, recent dental / surgical procedure, central venous catheter, haemodialysis.
redFlags: Decompensated heart failure (acute valve regurgitation) → urgent valve surgery.
Persistent fever despite > 7 days appropriate antibiotic — uncontrolled infection / abscess.
Embolic stroke + large vegetation > 10 mm → consider early surgery.
Prosthetic-valve IE — high mortality, specialist + early surgery.

diagnostics.test: Three sets of blood cultures (separate sites, 30 min apart) BEFORE antibiotics
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies organism in > 90 %; mandatory before empirical treatment.
First-line; sensitivity 60–75 % native valve, 50 % prosthetic.
Higher sensitivity 90 %+; mandatory if TTE non-diagnostic, prosthetic valve, suspected abscess.
Anaemia of chronic disease, raised inflammatory markers, microscopic haematuria.
Definite IE = 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor.

management.detail: Native valve: amoxicillin 2 g IV every 4 h + flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 h + gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 h. Prosthetic valve: vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin. Penicillin allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin. Duration 4–6 weeks (longer for prosthetic).

Adjust per culture + sensitivity. Common: viridans streptococci — penicillin G 12–18 MU/day IV for 4 weeks. S. aureus MSSA — flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 h for 4–6 weeks. Enterococcus — ampicillin + gentamicin OR ampicillin + ceftriaxone.

Heart failure from acute valve dysfunction (urgent), uncontrolled infection (persistent fever + bacteraemia > 7 days, perivalvular abscess, fungal IE), high embolic risk (large mobile vegetation > 10 mm + prior embolic event).
Cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, infectious disease, microbiology, radiology + dental specialist for source control.

Per ESC 2023 — only high-risk procedures in highest-risk patients: prior IE, prosthetic valve, congenital cyanotic heart disease, transplant valvulopathy. Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 min pre-procedure.

title: Rheumatic heart disease (chronic management)
presentation: Sequela of acute rheumatic fever (group A strep). Major SSA cardiac burden.
Mitral valve disease most common — mitral stenosis (MS) / mitral regurgitation (MR).
Symptoms: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, palpitations (AF), haemoptysis (MS pulmonary congestion), right HF.
Murmurs: MS — opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble at apex. MR — apical pansystolic radiating to axilla.
redFlags: AF + MS — extreme stroke risk (4–7 % per year without anticoagulation).
Pulmonary oedema in pregnancy + MS — emergency. Foetal / maternal mortality high.
Severe MS — mean gradient > 10 mmHg, valve area < 1.0 cm² — needs valvotomy / valve replacement.

diagnostics.rationale: Mandatory — valve morphology, gradient, area, LA size, pulmonary pressure, LV / RV function.
P mitrale (LA enlargement), AF, RV hypertrophy.
Cardiomegaly, LA enlargement, pulmonary congestion.

management.detail: Benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM every 21–28 days (600 000 IU if < 30 kg). Duration: 10 years OR until age 21 (whichever longer) if no carditis. 10 years OR until 40 if carditis without residual heart disease. Lifelong if carditis with residual valve disease. Alternatives: oral penicillin V 250 mg twice daily, OR erythromycin if penicillin allergic.
Diuretics for congestion. β-blocker for tachycardia / AF (avoid in severe MS — relies on diastolic time). Avoid ACE-i in severe MS.
Rate control + anticoagulation (warfarin — DOACs NOT validated in valvular AF with mitral stenosis). INR target 2.0–3.0.

Severe MS in pregnancy is high-risk. Pre-conception counselling + valvotomy where feasible. Multidisciplinary care: cardio-obstetric team. β-blocker for tachycardia, diuretic for pulmonary congestion. Avoid heparin in WHO IV — special protocols.
Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy for suitable rheumatic MS (mobile valve, no severe MR). Valve replacement for severe disease, MR, or unsuitable for valvotomy.
Treat all streptococcal pharyngitis with penicillin V 10 days. Improve living conditions (overcrowding reduction).

references.label: World Heart Federation Position on RHD

title: Ischaemic stroke / TIA — secondary prevention (adult)
presentation: Post-acute-stroke phase — secondary prevention begins within 24 h of stable presentation.
ABCD2 score for TIA risk-stratification of subsequent stroke.
Imaging mandatory to confirm ischaemic vs haemorrhagic before antithrombotic therapy.
redFlags: Within 24 h of thrombolysis / large-vessel occlusion — avoid antiplatelet (24 h) and anticoagulation (longer).
Recurrent stroke / TIA despite secondary prevention — escalate / investigate aetiology.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm ischaemic stroke + exclude haemorrhage.
Carotid stenosis > 50 % anterior circulation → CEA / CAS.
Detect AF — cryptogenic stroke; consider implantable loop recorder if high suspicion.

diagnostics.test: Lipid profile, HbA1c, fasting glucose, FBC, U&E, vasculitis screen if young / atypical
diagnostics.rationale: Risk factors + uncommon causes.
Embolic source.

management.detail: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily monotherapy first-line (CAPRIE). Alternative: aspirin 75 mg + dipyridamole 200 mg modified-release twice daily. Short-course dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel 21 days for minor stroke / high-risk TIA; CHANCE / POINT). Aspirin monotherapy second-line.
DOAC 14 days post-stroke (sooner for TIA / minor stroke). Avoid warfarin / DOAC for first 24 h after thrombolysis.
High-intensity atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg daily — LDL target < 1.8 mmol/L (or > 50 % reduction).
Target < 130/80 mmHg long-term (allow gradual reduction over 1–2 weeks post-stroke). ACE-i + thiazide / CCB combinations; avoid abrupt BP lowering in acute phase.
CEA within 2 weeks for symptomatic 70–99 % stenosis (or 50–69 % in selected); CAS alternative.
Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, weight loss, exercise, Mediterranean diet.
Early multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, psychology — start within 24–48 h of stable presentation.

references.label: AHA / ASA Secondary Stroke Prevention Guidelines (2021)

title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)
presentation: Heterozygous FH (HeFH) prevalence ~ 1:250. Untreated HeFH adult LDL 5–13 mmol/L; coronary events from 4th decade onwards.
Homozygous FH (HoFH, 1:300 000) — LDL > 13 mmol/L; coronary disease in childhood; tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus < 45 y.
Family history of premature CV disease (men < 55, women < 60), tendon xanthomata (Achilles, knuckles, dorsum of hand).
redFlags: LDL > 4.9 mmol/L or TC > 8.0 — investigate FH.
Tendon xanthoma or corneal arcus in a patient < 45 y — FH until proven otherwise.
Multiple first-degree relatives with premature CV events.
Suspected homozygous FH (LDL > 13, childhood xanthomata) — urgent specialist.

diagnostics.rationale: LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L in adult or ≥ 4.0 in child < 16 highly suggestive.
Combine LDL, family history, physical signs, genetic test.
LDLR / APOB / PCSK9 mutation — confirms diagnosis + cascade screening.
Exclude secondary hyperlipidaemia (hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis).
50 % heterozygosity rate; early diagnosis prevents premature CV death.

management.detail: Mediterranean diet, < 7 % saturated fat, soluble fibre, plant sterols, regular exercise, smoking cessation, weight optimisation.
Atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg. Aim ≥ 50 % LDL reduction. Adult LDL target < 2.6 mmol/L (or < 1.8 with CV disease).
10 mg daily — additional 15–20 % LDL reduction. Standard add-on if statin alone insufficient.
Alirocumab / evolocumab SC every 2–4 weeks — additional 50–60 % LDL reduction. Specialist; reserved for high-risk FH or statin-intolerant.
Start statin from age 8–10 (lower-intensity dosing). Specialist.
LDL apheresis + PCSK9 inhibitor + lomitapide or evinacumab. Liver transplantation considered.
Stop statins + ezetimibe + PCSK9i pre-conception + throughout pregnancy + breastfeeding. Cholestyramine for severe disease.

title: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT, adult)
presentation: Sudden-onset palpitations, often associated with anxiety, dyspnoea, chest discomfort, presyncope.
Heart rate typically 150–250 / min, regular, narrow QRS (unless aberrancy / pre-existing BBB).
Termination often abrupt with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine.
Mechanisms: AV-nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT — most common), AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT — accessory pathway / WPW), atrial tachycardia.
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability (SBP < 90, altered mental state, pulmonary oedema, ongoing chest pain) → emergency DC cardioversion 50–100 J biphasic.
Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) — wide irregular bizarre tachycardia → DO NOT give AV-nodal blockers; use procainamide or DC cardiovert.
Wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin — treat as VT until proven otherwise.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm narrow vs wide complex, regular vs irregular, P-wave morphology / position.

diagnostics.test: Resting ECG when in sinus rhythm
diagnostics.rationale: WPW (short PR, delta wave) — alters treatment.
Identify contributing factors.

management.detail: Valsalva (modified Valsalva better — REVERT trial: 15-s strain + supine + passive leg-raise; 43 % conversion). Carotid sinus massage (avoid in elderly / carotid bruit / stroke history). Diving reflex in young (cold-water face immersion).
6 mg rapid IV bolus + 20 mL flush into large vein. If no response in 2 min, 12 mg, then 12 mg. Counsel patient — transient flushing, chest pressure, sense of impending doom (lasts 10–20 sec).
Verapamil 5 mg IV slow over 2 min (avoid if HFrEF, β-blocker IV, WPW with AF) OR diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV. Repeat 15 min if needed.
Catheter ablation — curative for AVNRT / AVRT (> 95 % success); first-line in WPW. β-blocker / non-DHP CCB for prevention if ablation declined.
AVOID AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) — paradoxical acceleration via accessory pathway → VF. Use procainamide 50 mg/min IV (max 17 mg/kg) OR DC cardioversion.

title: Acute aortic dissection
presentation: Sudden tearing / ripping chest / interscapular / abdominal pain — most severe at onset.
May radiate or 'migrate' as dissection propagates.
Pulse deficit, > 20 mmHg BP difference between arms, new aortic regurgitation murmur, signs of branch occlusion (stroke, paraplegia, mesenteric ischaemia, limb ischaemia).
Risk: hypertension (90 %), connective tissue disorder (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos vascular), bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine use, pregnancy (peripartum), aortic surgery / catheterisation.
redFlags: ANY suspicion in young patient — high mortality if missed (1 % per hour mortality untreated for Stanford type A).
Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) — pericardial effusion from rupture.
Hemiplegia / paraplegia / mesenteric ischaemia — branch-vessel involvement.
Hypotension — rupture / tamponade; do NOT fluid-overload.

diagnostics.test: CT angiogram of chest, abdomen, pelvis
diagnostics.rationale: First-line diagnostic — extent + branch vessels. Sensitivity > 95 %.
Alternative if CT unavailable / contrast allergy; bedside in unstable patient.
Exclude STEMI (right coronary if dissection involves coronary ostium); usually non-specific.
Widened mediastinum (60–90 %), aortic knob abnormality. Normal does NOT exclude.

diagnostics.test: FBC, U&E, lactate, troponin, D-dimer (high NPV when low)
diagnostics.rationale: Severity + alternative diagnoses.

management.detail: ABCDE. Two large-bore IV access. Cross-match 6 units RBC. Pain control — IV morphine titrated. Do NOT thrombolyse if mimicking STEMI.

Target SBP 100–120 mmHg + HR < 60 to reduce shear stress. IV β-blocker FIRST (esmolol 500 µg/kg load + 50 µg/kg/min infusion, OR labetalol 20 mg IV repeated to max 300 mg). Add nitroprusside / GTN infusion if BP still elevated AFTER β-blockade. Never use vasodilator alone — reflex tachycardia worsens dissection.
Surgical emergency — cardiothoracic surgery for graft replacement. Mortality 1 % per hour untreated.
Medical management with BP + HR control. Endovascular stent (TEVAR) if complicated (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain / hypertension).
Marfan + aortic root > 4 cm — surveillance + β-blocker. Acute dissection in pregnancy — maternal salvage takes priority; type A → surgery + caesarean if foetus viable.
Lifelong BP control (target < 120/80), β-blocker, surveillance CT / MR every 6–12 months. Counsel against weightlifting, contact sports.

title: Acute pericarditis (adult)
presentation: Sharp pleuritic chest pain (worse on inspiration, lying flat, relieved leaning forward).
Pericardial friction rub (best heard left sternal edge with patient leaning forward).
May coexist with myocarditis (myopericarditis) → raised troponin.
Causes: viral / idiopathic (80–90 %), TB (high SSA prevalence — especially with HIV), uraemic, post-MI (Dressler), autoimmune, malignancy, post-cardiac-surgery.
redFlags: Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg → emergency pericardiocentesis.
Large effusion (> 20 mm anechoic space) — admit + close monitoring.
Constrictive pericarditis (chronic TB or radiation) — Kussmaul sign, pulsus paradoxus, hepatomegaly, ascites — refer for pericardiectomy.
Suspected TB pericarditis (SSA) — admit, urgent investigations + empirical anti-TB therapy.

diagnostics.rationale: Diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression (early); T-wave inversion (later). Distinguish from STEMI (regional ST elevation + reciprocal depression).
Pericardial effusion, tamponade physiology, myocardial involvement.
Inflammation, myopericarditis, uraemic / hypothyroid causes.

diagnostics.test: CXR + targeted: HIV, IGRA, blood culture, autoimmune screen, malignancy screen
diagnostics.rationale: Cause-directed.
Tamponade therapy + diagnostic — TB culture / NAAT / cytology / biochemistry.

management.detail: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 1–2 weeks (taper) OR aspirin 750–1000 mg three times daily. ADD colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months (reduces recurrence — COPE / CORP trials). PPI cover.
Refrain from strenuous physical activity until resolution of symptoms + normalisation of CRP + ECG + echo (typically 3 months). Athletes — longer.
Reserve for NSAID failure / contraindication / autoimmune cause / pregnancy 3rd trimester. Increases recurrence. Prednisolone 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day taper over 3 months.

Standard 4-drug anti-TB therapy (2HRZE / 4HR or 6 months) + adjunctive prednisolone (controversial — IMPI trial showed no mortality benefit but reduced constriction). Consider pericardiectomy if constriction develops.
Continue colchicine 6–12 months. Add IL-1 blocker (anakinra, rilonacept) for refractory specialist.
Urgent pericardiocentesis (echo-guided ideal); avoid IPPV (worsens haemodynamics). IV fluids cautiously; do NOT use diuretics (preload-dependent).

title: Cardiogenic shock (adult)
presentation: Hypotension (SBP < 90 sustained > 30 min OR requiring vasopressor to maintain MAP ≥ 65) + signs of end-organ hypoperfusion (cool clammy extremities, oliguria < 30 mL/h, altered mental state, lactate > 2 mmol/L).
Most common cause: acute MI (especially STEMI / large infarct) — 5–8 % of MI patients.
Other causes: severe acute valve dysfunction (rupture, IE), arrhythmia, acute myocarditis, end-stage HF, mechanical complication of MI (VSR, papillary rupture, free wall rupture).
SCAI classification A–E for severity.
redFlags: Mechanical complication of MI — sudden new murmur + decompensation → emergency echo + surgery.
Refractory shock despite inotropes / vasopressors → mechanical circulatory support consideration.
Right heart failure / RV infarct — preload-dependent; avoid diuretics + nitrates.

diagnostics.rationale: STEMI / NSTEMI / arrhythmia identification.
EF, regional wall motion, valvular complications, RV function, pericardial effusion, mechanical defects.

diagnostics.test: Lactate + ABG, FBC, U&E, lactate, LFT, coagulation
diagnostics.rationale: Severity + end-organ damage.
Pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly, aortic outline.
Mandatory for ACS-related shock — primary PCI within hours.

management.detail: Airway, oxygen target SpO₂ 94–98 % (caution in pure RV — preload-dependent). NIV / intubation for respiratory failure. Two large-bore IV. Cross-match 4 units.
250 mL crystalloid bolus only if no pulmonary oedema and suspected hypovolaemia component. STOP if no response or SpO₂ falls. RV infarct — generous fluids (500–1000 mL).

Noradrenaline 0.05–0.5 µg/kg/min titrated to MAP ≥ 65 (first-line per SOAP-II trial — better than dopamine). Add dobutamine 2.5–10 µg/kg/min as inotrope OR milrinone 0.25–0.75 µg/kg/min (avoid in renal failure / hypotension).

STEMI: primary PCI within 90 min + dual antiplatelet. NSTEMI: PCI within 24 h. Massive PE: thrombolysis / embolectomy. Mechanical complication: urgent surgery. Arrhythmia: cardioversion / antiarrhythmic. Sepsis-related: full sepsis bundle.
Intra-aortic balloon pump (limited evidence post-IABP-SHOCK II). VA-ECMO + Impella for refractory / bridge to recovery / transplant. Specialist centre referral early.
Arterial line, central venous line, urinary catheter. Renal replacement therapy if AKI. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis, VTE prophylaxis. Sedation if intubated. Multi-disciplinary cardiac team.

title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)
presentation: Most are asymptomatic — detected on screening / incidental imaging.
Symptomatic but unruptured: vague abdominal / back pain, pulsatile abdominal mass.
Ruptured AAA — triad of severe abdominal / back pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass; high mortality (50–80 %).
Risk factors: smoking (strongest), age > 65, male, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis, COPD, connective-tissue disease.
redFlags: Suspected ruptured AAA — DO NOT delay for imaging if hypotensive + classic features → vascular surgery directly.
Aortic-enteric fistula — GI bleeding in patient with known AAA / repair → emergency.
Rapidly expanding AAA (> 1 cm / year) → urgent vascular review.

diagnostics.rationale: First-line screening — sensitivity 95 % for AAA > 3 cm.
Confirms diagnosis, dimensions, branch involvement, planning for repair.
UK NAAASP, US USPSTF — one-off abdominal USS for men aged 65–75 with smoking history.

management.detail: 3.0–4.4 cm: annual ultrasound. 4.5–5.4 cm: 6-monthly ultrasound. Symptomatic OR > 1 cm/year growth — refer vascular for repair.

Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) — preferred for anatomically suitable + higher-risk patients; less initial mortality. Open repair — anatomically unsuitable / younger fitter patients; durability advantage. Vascular surgery.
Smoking cessation (strongest predictor of growth). BP target < 130/80 mmHg with β-blocker (some evidence of slower expansion). Statin + aspirin per CV risk.
Permissive hypotension (SBP 70–90 mmHg) until clamp in theatre. Cross-match 10 units. Urgent vascular surgery — EVAR or open repair. AVOID over-aggressive fluid resuscitation (worsens bleeding).
EVAR: CT at 1 month, 6 months, 1 year, then annually (endoleak risk). Open repair: less intensive — 5-yearly CT.

title: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (adult)
presentation: Cough, fever, dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, sputum production.
CURB-65 ≥ 3 OR SMART-COP ≥ 5 OR major IDSA/ATS criteria (septic shock requiring vasopressor, respiratory failure requiring ventilation, OR ≥ 3 minor criteria).
Common organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus aureus (post-influenza).
redFlags: Septic shock — refractory hypotension after fluids.
Respiratory failure — RR > 30, SpO₂ < 88 % on room air, PaO₂/FiO₂ < 250.
Bilateral pneumonia in immunocompromised → consider PJP (HIV) — add cotrimoxazole.

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm + extent; cavitation; pleural effusion.
Severity + organ dysfunction.
Yield 5–14 % in severe CAP; guides therapy.

diagnostics.test: Sputum Gram stain + culture, Legionella urinary antigen, pneumococcal urinary antigen
diagnostics.rationale: Pathogen identification.

diagnostics.test: HIV test + nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 / influenza / RSV
diagnostics.rationale: Identifies treatable causes + co-infections.

management.detail: SpO₂ target 94–98 % (88–92 % in COPD risk). High-flow / NIV / intubation per severity. Consider HDU/ICU.

First-line: IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g every 8 h + clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 h (or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily). For ICU: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily + clarithromycin OR levofloxacin 750 mg once daily monotherapy. MRSA cover (vancomycin) if recent influenza + cavitation. Pseudomonas cover (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftazidime) if bronchiectasis / recent hospitalisation.
30 mL/kg crystalloid (Ringer's lactate preferred) for hypotension / lactate ≥ 4. Vasopressors (noradrenaline) for MAP < 65 despite fluids.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV continuous infusion for 4–8 days in patients with septic shock + severe CAP (CAPE-COD trial, ESCMID 2023).

Tailor to organism / sensitivities at 48–72 h. Step down to oral when afebrile + improving. Total duration 5–7 days for uncomplicated; longer for complicated (empyema, abscess, S. aureus, Legionella).
Pneumococcal + influenza vaccination. Smoking cessation. Repeat CXR at 6 weeks (resolution; exclude underlying malignancy in smokers > 50).

title: Acute bacterial meningitis (adult, detailed)
presentation: Classic triad (only 44 %): fever + neck stiffness + altered mental state.
Headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting.
Petechial / purpuric rash → meningococcal.
Common organisms: S. pneumoniae (most common), N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, Listeria (elderly / immunocompromised / pregnant).
redFlags: Septic shock + purpura fulminans (meningococcal sepsis) → IV ceftriaxone within minutes — do NOT delay for LP.
Raised intracranial pressure / focal signs / seizure / GCS < 12 → CT before LP.
Suspected TB meningitis (HIV, subacute presentation, basal meningeal enhancement) → start anti-TB empirically alongside antibiotics.

diagnostics.rationale: Yield ~ 70 % — definitive identification.

CSF: opening pressure (typically > 25 cmH₂O), cell count + differential, glucose (CSF:plasma < 0.4), protein > 1 g/L, Gram stain + culture, PCR (meningococcal / pneumococcal / HSV / TB), lactate > 4 mmol/L bacterial.
Immunocompromised, focal neurology, seizure, papilloedema, GCS < 12. Otherwise NOT routinely required.

diagnostics.test: HIV test, FBC, U&E, glucose, CRP, lactate, coagulation, CXR
diagnostics.rationale: Severity + co-morbidity.

management.detail: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h × 4 days, FIRST OR within 15 min of first antibiotic dose (reduces neurologic complications in pneumococcal meningitis). PLUS IV ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h + amoxicillin 2 g every 4 h (Listeria cover in > 50 y / immunocompromised / pregnant). Add vancomycin in regions with penicillin-resistant pneumococcus. PLUS aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h if HSV suspected.
ICU admission. Maintain MAP ≥ 70. Glucose 8–10 mmol/L. Treat seizures. NG feeding if obtunded. DVT prophylaxis.

Statutory notification within 24 h. Meningococcal disease: ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose OR rifampicin 600 mg every 12 h × 2 days for close contacts (household, kissing partners). Vaccinate non-immune close contacts.
Pneumococcus — penicillin if sensitive. Meningococcus — penicillin G. Listeria — amoxicillin + gentamicin. Duration 7–14 days (pneumococcus / meningococcus) or 21 days (Listeria / Gram-negative).

management.step: Hearing assessment + neurological review at 6 weeks
management.detail: 20–30 % have neurologic sequelae (cognitive, motor, sensorineural deafness). Audiology before discharge + 6 weeks.

title: Viral encephalitis (adult)
presentation: Fever + altered mental state + headache + new neurologic deficit / seizure.
Personality / behaviour change, dysphasia, focal weakness, ataxia.

Common causes: HSV-1 (most common identifiable), HSV-2 (genital tract reactivation), VZV, enterovirus, arboviruses (Japanese encephalitis, West Nile, dengue in tropics), CMV / EBV in immunocompromised.
redFlags: Temporal-lobe focal features (memory, behavioural change, dysphasia) → HSV-1 in 60–90 %. Start aciclovir IMMEDIATELY.
Immunocompromised + altered mental state — broaden differential (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, PML, CMV).

diagnostics.rationale: Temporal + frontal lobe involvement = HSV-1.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly raised protein, normal glucose, RBC (HSV-1 haemorrhagic), HSV / VZV / enterovirus PCR.
Temporal-lobe periodic discharges in HSV-1 (PLEDs).

diagnostics.test: HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, cryptococcal antigen, autoimmune encephalitis panel (NMDA-R, LGI1, CASPR2)
diagnostics.rationale: Differential diagnosis.

management.detail: 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h infused over 1 h × 14–21 days. Adjust for renal function. Reduces mortality + morbidity in HSV from 70 % → 28 % (untreated 70 %).
While distinguishing from meningitis: empirical ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h + amoxicillin (Listeria) + dexamethasone — stop when bacterial cause excluded.
Levetiracetam 1500 mg IV (or phenytoin 20 mg/kg) for active seizures. Continuous EEG if status / refractory.
Airway, oxygenation, glucose, electrolytes, IV fluids. Mechanical ventilation if airway compromise.
Trial of high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily × 5 days + IVIG / plasma exchange if antibody-mediated suspected.
Neuropsychology + occupational + speech therapy. Chronic epilepsy in 25 %. Psychiatric / cognitive impairment common.

title: Necrotising fasciitis / necrotising soft-tissue infection
presentation: Pain DISPROPORTIONATE to physical findings — hallmark early sign.
Rapidly spreading erythema → dusky / violaceous → bullae → frank necrosis.
Systemic toxicity: fever, tachycardia, hypotension out of proportion to local infection.
Crepitus on palpation (gas-forming organisms).
Types: I — polymicrobial (diabetes, post-surgery, perineum [Fournier]). II — Group A strep (any age, no risk factor). III — marine exposure (Vibrio vulnificus). IV — fungal.
redFlags: ANY suspicion = SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Mortality 25–35 %; rises to > 70 % if surgery delayed > 24 h.

diagnostics.rationale: Lack of normal tissue resistance + dishwater discharge = diagnosis. Imaging should NOT delay surgery.

diagnostics.test: LRINEC score (CRP > 150, WCC > 15, Hb < 13.5, Na < 135, creatinine > 141 µmol/L, glucose > 10)
diagnostics.rationale: Risk stratification — but normal does not exclude.
Gas in fascial planes, fascial thickening — useful only if patient stable + diagnosis uncertain.
Organism identification — guide antimicrobial de-escalation.

management.detail: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 h (or carbapenem) + clindamycin 900 mg every 8 h (toxin suppression) + vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 h (MRSA cover). Adjust per culture. Duration ≥ 14 days post-final debridement.
MUST be within 6 hours of recognition. Aggressive removal of all necrotic tissue. Repeat 'second look' surgery within 24 h. Mortality reduced from > 70 % to 4–12 % with early surgery.
Crystalloid resuscitation, vasopressor if shock, blood products for DIC. ICU mandatory.
Hyperbaric oxygen + IVIG (toxic-shock GAS) — adjuncts where available; do not delay surgery for either.
Long-term wound management — vacuum-assisted closure (VAC), skin grafting, plastic reconstruction. Rehabilitation. Psychological support — disfigurement common.

references.label: IDSA Skin + Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines 2014

title: Septic arthritis (adult)
presentation: Acute hot swollen painful joint, restricted range of motion, fever.
Usually monoarticular (knee > hip > shoulder).
Risk: pre-existing joint disease (RA, OA), diabetes, immunosuppression, IVDU, recent intra-articular injection, prosthetic joint, distant focus (bacteraemia).
Common organisms: S. aureus (50 %), streptococci (25 %), Gram-negative (elderly / immunocompromised / IVDU), gonococcus (young sexually active).
redFlags: Hip / shoulder involvement — increased complications (avascular necrosis, axial bacteraemia).
Prosthetic joint — extended treatment, orthopaedic involvement essential.
Polyarticular involvement — gonococcus / SLE flare / IE / viral / Lyme.

diagnostics.rationale: WCC > 50 × 10⁹/L (often > 100), neutrophil > 75 %, Gram stain (positive 30–50 %), culture (gold standard).
Positive 50 % — guides therapy.
Baseline; rules out osteomyelitis / foreign body.
Hip joint, deep / difficult joints, suspected osteomyelitis.

management.detail: Native joint: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 h + (if MRSA risk) vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 h. Gonococcus suspected: ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 h. Step down to oral when stable + adjusted to culture. Total duration 4–6 weeks (2 weeks IV).
Repeated needle aspiration (8 hourly initially) OR arthroscopic / open washout — orthopaedic referral. Hip / shoulder almost always surgical.
Splint in functional position 48 h then gentle mobilisation to prevent stiffness. NSAID + paracetamol for pain. AVOID intra-articular steroids.
Multidisciplinary — orthopaedic + ID. Often requires DAIR (debridement + retention + 6-week IV antibiotics) OR 2-stage exchange revision arthroplasty.
Physiotherapy from day 2. Long-term follow-up for joint function + recurrence risk.

title: Osteomyelitis (adult)
presentation: Acute: localised bone pain + fever + erythema + reduced range of motion.
Chronic: prolonged pain, draining sinus, recurrent infection.
Vertebral osteomyelitis: back pain + tenderness + neurological deficit (myelopathy) + fever (often subtle).
Risk: open fracture, surgery, prosthetic joint, diabetic foot ulcer, pressure ulcer, IVDU, contiguous spread, haematogenous (S. aureus most common).
redFlags: Vertebral osteomyelitis with neurological deficit — emergency MRI + neurosurgical assessment.
Septic shock — severe haematogenous OM or contiguous-source sepsis.
Diabetic foot OM — high amputation risk.
Brodie abscess — chronic OM with abscess; may need surgical drainage.

diagnostics.rationale: Most sensitive imaging — marrow oedema, abscess, sinus tract.
Gold standard — guides antibiotic choice. Hold antibiotics 2 weeks before biopsy where feasible.
Severity + monitor response. CRP halves with effective treatment by week 2.
Baseline — bone changes lag clinical disease by 10–14 days.

management.detail: Acute haematogenous: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 h + (MRSA risk) vancomycin. Vertebral: IV flucloxacillin OR vancomycin + ceftriaxone. Diabetic foot: piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin. Switch to oral when stable + susceptibilities. Total duration 6 weeks (vertebral / haematogenous) to 12 weeks (diabetic foot / chronic). Suppressive therapy 6–12 months for prosthesis retention.
Often needed — sequestrum, dead bone, abscess, fistula. Always for prosthetic joint OM (DAIR vs revision). Vertebral with abscess / cord compression → urgent decompression.
Treat diabetic foot ulcer (off-loading, revascularisation), pressure ulcer, oral hygiene if dental seeding.
CRP / ESR weekly for first month then monthly. Repeat MRI at 3 months if not responding. Bone scan unhelpful early (post-op uptake).
Multidisciplinary — orthopaedics, ID, vascular, plastic surgery, podiatry. Recurrence may occur years later — counsel + monitor.

title: Neutropenic fever (febrile neutropenia, adult)
presentation: Single temperature ≥ 38.3 °C OR sustained ≥ 38.0 °C for ≥ 1 h, with absolute neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10⁹/L (or < 1.0 with anticipated fall to < 0.5).
Often occurs 7–10 days post-chemotherapy (nadir).
Source identifiable in only 20–30 % (catheter, mucositis, pneumonia, perianal, urinary, skin).
Most common organisms: Gram-negative bacteraemia (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas), Gram-positive (coag-neg staph, viridans strep), fungal (later in course).
redFlags: MASCC score < 21 — high risk; admit for IV.
Profound prolonged neutropenia (ANC < 0.1 for > 7 days) — fungal infection risk.
Visible perianal pain / induration — perianal abscess (avoid DRE — bacteraemia risk).

diagnostics.rationale: Confirm neutrophil count.

diagnostics.test: Blood cultures × 2 (peripheral + each lumen of central line) BEFORE antibiotics
diagnostics.rationale: Yield 20–30 %.

diagnostics.test: Urinalysis + culture, sputum culture, wound swab, CXR
diagnostics.rationale: Source identification.

diagnostics.test: U&E, CRP, LFT, lactate, glucose, coagulation, ABG (sepsis)
diagnostics.rationale: Severity + organ function.
Low-risk: outpatient oral therapy. High-risk: IV in-patient.

management.detail: High-risk: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 h (or meropenem if recent ESBL / severe sepsis). Add vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 h if septic shock, MRSA risk, mucositis, line infection. Antifungal (caspofungin / liposomal amphotericin) at day 4–7 if persistent fever despite broad antibiotic.
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 8 h + amoxicillin-clavulanate 625 mg every 8 h. 24-h observation + close follow-up.
Remove infected central line if confirmed line sepsis (especially if Candida / S. aureus / Pseudomonas).
Fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support if shock. G-CSF (filgrastim) NOT routinely indicated; reserve for severe sepsis / prolonged neutropenia.
After 48–72 h: review culture + sensitivities, narrow spectrum. Stop antibiotics when afebrile ≥ 48 h + ANC recovering > 0.5. Total duration ≥ 7 days for documented infection.

title: Acute pyelonephritis (adult)
presentation: Fever, rigors, loin pain, costovertebral angle tenderness.
