presentation: A puncture, laceration or crush wound from an animal or human bite.
Cat bites cause deep puncture wounds with high infection risk (Pasteurella); human bites risk Eikenella and viral transmission.
Signs of infection (redness, swelling, discharge) may develop over 24–72 hours.
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, abscess, tenosynovitis or joint/bone involvement.
Rabies risk (assess exposure and need for post-exposure prophylaxis).
Clenched-fist 'fight-bite' injuries over the knuckles (joint penetration).

diagnostics.rationale: Assess depth, structures involved (tendon, joint, nerve) and contamination.
Detect fractures, retained teeth or joint involvement.

management.detail: Copious irrigation and debridement; generally leave high-risk bite wounds open or delay primary closure (especially cat/human bites and hands).
Co-amoxiclav is first-line prophylaxis/treatment; assess tetanus status and rabies post-exposure prophylaxis based on the animal and region; consider hepatitis B/HIV risk for human bites.
Review for infection; refer hand/joint involvement to surgery.

title: Iron poisoning
presentation: Stages: early GI toxicity (vomiting, diarrhoea, GI bleeding), an apparent latent period, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure and late strictures.
Common in young children ingesting iron tablets/supplements.
Severity relates to elemental iron dose (mg/kg).
redFlags: Shock, coma, severe metabolic acidosis or persistent vomiting.
High serum iron level or radio-opaque tablets on X-ray.

diagnostics.rationale: Guides severity and need for chelation.
Radio-opaque tablets confirm ingestion; assess acidosis and organ injury.

management.detail: Aggressive IV fluids; whole-bowel irrigation for significant ingestions or visible tablets (activated charcoal does NOT bind iron).
IV desferrioxamine for severe toxicity (shock, acidosis, high iron level, significant symptoms).
Manage acidosis, coagulopathy and hepatic failure; monitor for late GI strictures.

title: Digoxin toxicity
presentation: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion and visual disturbance (yellow-green halos).
Bradyarrhythmias and almost any tachy/brady-arrhythmia (classically with AV block).
Acute overdose vs chronic toxicity (often older patients with renal impairment).
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia in acute toxicity (marker of severity).

diagnostics.test: Serum digoxin level, potassium and renal function
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm toxicity; potassium guides prognosis/treatment in acute overdose.
Detect characteristic arrhythmias and conduction block.

management.detail: Give digoxin immune Fab for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia, or haemodynamic instability.
Correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia; atropine and temporary pacing for bradycardia; treat ventricular arrhythmia (avoid calcium in hyperkalaemia from digoxin).
Activated charcoal if early after acute ingestion with a protected airway.

title: Beta-blocker / calcium-channel-blocker overdose
presentation: Bradycardia and hypotension after overdose of a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker.
Beta-blockers: bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia, seizures (especially lipophilic agents). CCBs: hyperglycaemia, preserved consciousness despite shock.
Conduction block and cardiogenic shock.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect bradycardia, conduction block and QRS/QT changes.
Hyperglycaemia suggests CCB toxicity; guides high-dose insulin therapy.

management.detail: IV fluids, atropine, calcium (for CCB), and glucagon (for beta-blockers); decontamination/whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release ingestions.
High-dose insulin with glucose is a key inotropic therapy for significant CCB (and beta-blocker) toxicity; monitor glucose and potassium.
Vasopressors, IV lipid emulsion for lipophilic agents, transvenous pacing and mechanical circulatory support for refractory shock.

references.label: TOXBASE / national poisons guidance — beta-blockers and calcium-channel blockers

title: High-altitude illness (AMS, HACE, HAPE)
presentation: Acute mountain sickness: headache, nausea, fatigue and poor sleep after rapid ascent above ~2500 m.
High-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE): ataxia, confusion, reduced consciousness.
High-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE): breathlessness at rest, cough, reduced exercise tolerance, frothy sputum.
redFlags: Failure to improve or worsening despite rest.

diagnostics.test: Clinical diagnosis based on altitude and symptoms
diagnostics.rationale: History of recent ascent with typical features is sufficient.
Detect hypoxia and pulmonary crackles (HAPE).

management.detail: Immediate descent is the definitive treatment for HACE and HAPE; stop further ascent for AMS.
Oxygen/portable hyperbaric chamber; acetazolamide for AMS prevention/treatment, dexamethasone for HACE, nifedipine for HAPE.
Gradual ascent, acclimatisation, and prophylaxis (acetazolamide) for susceptible individuals.

references.label: Wilderness Medical Society guidelines for acute altitude illness

title: Electrical injury
presentation: Burns at entry and exit points after contact with an electrical source; deep tissue damage may exceed surface findings.
Cardiac arrhythmia, especially after high-voltage or lightning injury.
Possible loss of consciousness, falls and associated trauma.
redFlags: Compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis from deep muscle injury.

diagnostics.rationale: Detect arrhythmia; monitor high-voltage/symptomatic patients.
Identify rhabdomyolysis and risk of pigment nephropathy.

management.detail: Isolate the power source before contact; ALS for arrest (prolonged resuscitation may be warranted in lightning).
Generous IV fluids if significant tissue injury/rhabdomyolysis to maintain urine output.
Treat burns, watch for compartment syndrome, assess for occult deep injury and associated trauma; tetanus prophylaxis.

references.label: Burns and trauma guidance on electrical injuries

title: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIADH)
presentation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and inappropriately high urine sodium.
Often asymptomatic; nausea, confusion or seizures if severe/rapid.
Causes: CNS disease, lung pathology, malignancy, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine).

diagnostics.test: Paired serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium
diagnostics.rationale: Inappropriately concentrated urine with high urine sodium in a euvolaemic, hyponatraemic patient supports SIADH after excluding other causes.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, which mimic SIADH.

management.detail: Hypertonic (3%) saline for seizures/coma, with strict limits on correction rate.
First-line for chronic SIADH; treat the underlying cause and stop offending drugs.
Consider vasopressin-receptor antagonists (vaptans) or other agents under specialist guidance if restriction fails.

title: Diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency/resistance)
presentation: Polyuria with dilute urine and polydipsia; nocturia.
Central (AVP deficiency, e.g. post-pituitary surgery/trauma) or nephrogenic (AVP resistance, e.g. lithium, hypercalcaemia).
Risk of hypernatraemia if access to water is limited.
redFlags: Hypernatraemia and dehydration, especially if unable to drink.

diagnostics.test: Paired serum/urine osmolality (+/- water deprivation test)
diagnostics.rationale: Demonstrates inability to concentrate urine; copeptin/desmopressin response distinguishes central from nephrogenic.

diagnostics.test: Calcium, potassium, glucose and drug review
diagnostics.rationale: Identify reversible causes of nephrogenic DI and exclude osmotic diuresis.

management.detail: Allow free access to fluids; in acute/inpatient settings replace water deficit and monitor sodium closely.
Desmopressin replacement, titrated to symptoms and sodium.
Remove the cause (e.g. lithium), correct calcium/potassium; low-salt diet and thiazide +/- amiloride to reduce urine output.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology guidance on diabetes insipidus

title: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)
presentation: Hypertension that is resistant to treatment, often with hypokalaemia.
May be normokalaemic; muscle weakness, cramps and polyuria when potassium is low.
An under-recognised, treatable cause of secondary hypertension.

diagnostics.rationale: Screening test (raised aldosterone with suppressed renin); withdraw interfering drugs where possible.

diagnostics.test: Confirmatory testing and adrenal imaging +/- vein sampling
diagnostics.rationale: Confirm autonomous secretion and distinguish unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia.

management.detail: Spironolactone (or eplerenone) controls blood pressure and corrects hypokalaemia, especially in bilateral disease.
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy can cure or improve hypertension from a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma.
Track blood pressure, potassium and renal function; manage cardiovascular risk.

references.label: Endocrine Society guideline on primary aldosteronism

title: Cushing syndrome
presentation: Weight gain with central obesity, moon face, dorsocervical fat pad and proximal myopathy.
Purple striae, easy bruising, hypertension, glucose intolerance and mood change.
Commonest cause is exogenous corticosteroids; endogenous causes include pituitary (Cushing disease), adrenal and ectopic ACTH.
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia and very high cortisol (ectopic ACTH/malignancy).

diagnostics.rationale: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol.
Distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent causes and localises the source.

management.detail: Taper exogenous steroids where possible; surgery (transsphenoidal for pituitary, adrenalectomy for adrenal) for endogenous disease.
Steroidogenesis inhibitors to lower cortisol while awaiting/if unsuitable for surgery (specialist-led).
Treat hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, thromboprophylaxis and infection risk.

references.label: Endocrine Society guideline on Cushing syndrome

title: Acromegaly
presentation: Insidious enlargement of the hands, feet and facial features (coarsening, prognathism); ring/shoe size increase.
Headache, visual field defects, sweating, arthralgia and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Usually from a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma.
redFlags: Visual field loss from chiasmal compression.

diagnostics.test: Serum IGF-1 and oral glucose tolerance test with GH
diagnostics.rationale: Raised IGF-1 and failure of GH to suppress confirm the diagnosis.
Localises the adenoma and assesses chiasmal compression.

management.detail: Transsphenoidal resection is first-line for most adenomas.
Somatostatin analogues (e.g. octreotide/lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist or dopamine agonists when surgery is incomplete or unsuitable.
Monitor for residual disease, hypopituitarism, cardiovascular risk, sleep apnoea and colonoscopy surveillance.
